name: Ray Peat diet
lead: The Ray Peat diet is an eating pattern drawn from the writings of Raymond Peat (1936-2022), an American biologist who wrote about nutrition, hormones and aging. Followers call it "pro-metabolic" or "bioenergetic": the aim is to keep metabolic rate high, which they say supports thyroid function, hormone balance, energy and body composition. Typical foods are whole milk, cheese, ripe fruit and fruit juice, honey and sugar, root vegetables, eggs, shellfish, gelatin and broth, and saturated fats such as coconut oil and butter, while polyunsaturated fats from seed oils, nuts and fatty fish are avoided.[1][7][11][12][13]

People in appearance communities follow it for skin, leanness, hair and general vitality, through a chain proponents set out in their own terms: less polyunsaturated fat and more readily burned sugar are said to support the thyroid and a higher metabolic rate; a higher metabolic rate is said to bring hormone balance and lower stress hormones; and that balance is expected to show in skin quality, body composition and energy. Some forum members extend the framework to claims about testosterone, estrogen and even height.[1][5]

Peat published through articles on his website, a newsletter and a handful of books, and his ideas spread through discussion forums, podcasts and social media, especially after his death in November 2022.[9][10][14][15] The diet is documented in community guides and resource threads on looksmax.org that compile his writings on metabolic rate, sodium and water retention, and nicotine.[2][3][4][7] Dietitians and critics, including a 2005 reply from the Weston A. Price Foundation, dispute several of its premises, and no clinical trial has tested the diet as a whole.[16]

paras: As summarised in a looksmax.org post quoting a hospital dietitian, the diet emphasises healthy saturated fats, a heavy share of dairy, abundant fresh fruit and juice, root vegetables, animal protein and collagen. Followers cite the instability of polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs) to explain why they are excluded.[1]

One long guide on looksmax.org presents itself as condensing and organising Peat's scattered work to make it practical. Its author writes that few things are strongly advised apart from removing polyunsaturated fats and limiting starches, or making sure they are well cooked and eaten with fat, and that the most controversial ideas are the rejection of "essential" fatty acids and the promotion of refined sugar. The guide invites readers to adopt as much or as little as is practical.[7]

Community resource threads gather Peat's writings on metabolic rate and hormones, on sodium and water retention, and on nicotine.[2][3][4] Because Peat wrote as a researcher-essayist rather than a diet author, there is no single canonical menu; followers assemble the diet from articles such as those on milk, sugar, coconut oil and unsaturated fats.[10]

According to the biography on his website, Peat held a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon, specialised in physiology, and began work on progesterone and related hormones in 1968. He published papers in the journal Physiological Chemistry and Physics in 1971 and 1972, completed his dissertation in 1972, and taught at several institutions including the University of Oregon, Montana State University and the National College of Naturopathic Medicine. He also offered private nutritional counselling and painted portraits.[9] Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, adds that he was born on 12 October 1936 in Santee, California, earned a master's degree in humanities with a thesis on William Blake, and wrote a 1972 dissertation on oxidative changes in the hamster uterus.[14]

Peat's books, as listed by Grokipedia, include Nutrition for Women (1973), Mind and Tissue (1976), Progesterone in Orthomolecular Medicine (1993) and From PMS to Menopause (1997), published largely through his own imprint. He distributed a newsletter and posted articles at raypeat.com, whose pages carry copyright dates from 2006.[9][14] The site's article index covers topics such as progesterone, estrogen, thyroid, serotonin, cancer, sugar, salt, milk, unsaturated fats, coconut oil and aging.[10]

Peat died on 24 November 2022 at age 86. An obituary in the online magazine IM-1776 described his work as a "truly cosmological science" that drew on Soviet and American biology and on classical thinkers; its author argued that his ideas are often reduced to simplified diets and protocols.[15]

sections.h: Core ideas as stated by Peat and followers
paras: Metabolic rate and thyroid. Peat's framework treats a high rate of oxidative energy production as the basis of health, with thyroid hormone as a key driver and stress hormones, estrogen and polyunsaturated fats as suppressors. His site's article index includes a piece on TSH, temperature, pulse rate and other indicators in hypothyroidism, reflecting his interest in those measures as signs of thyroid function.[10]

Polyunsaturated fats. In his article on unsaturated fatty acids, Peat argues that PUFAs are not nutritionally essential but harmful. He disputes the early twentieth-century experiments used to establish essential fatty acids, attributing the reported deficiency symptoms to shortages of other nutrients, and links PUFA breakdown products to oxidative damage, thyroid suppression and age-related disease. He favours saturated and monounsaturated fats such as coconut oil.[11]

Sugar. In his article on sugar issues, Peat argues that sugar, and fructose in particular, is not the cause of obesity or diabetes, that these conditions reflect impaired sugar metabolism under stress, and that fruit, juice and honey are preferred sources; refined sugar is described as a more limited, occasional tool. He argues that starch and seed oils contribute more to fat gain than sugar does.[12]

Milk and calcium. Peat's article on milk presents dairy as a nutritionally sound food whose calcium he links to lower parathyroid hormone and, in his reading, less body fat. He defends milk against allergy and lactose-intolerance concerns and prefers whole milk.[13]

Other positions. Grokipedia summarises further Peat positions, including a preference for gelatin, shellfish and eggs, coffee as a beneficial food, scepticism toward endurance exercise, and a favourable view of aspirin and some antihistamines. It also notes his warnings against foods such as avocado, which it says lack support. Because that page is AI-generated, these points are best checked against Peat's own articles.[14]

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: Appearance-focused followers adopt the diet for the outcomes they associate with a high metabolic rate: warmer body temperature, energy for training, clearer skin, a leaner body composition and fuller-looking hair. In forum threads these goals sit alongside broader hormone-optimisation topics, and members debate which parts of the framework to apply.[1][2][7]

A pattern described in community guides is to build meals around dairy, fruit or juice, a cooked root vegetable or white rice, and eggs or shellfish, and to cook with saturated fats rather than seed oils. Some members also take up topics collected in the resource threads, such as Peat's views on dietary sodium and on nicotine.[3][4]

Forum members discuss the diet for hormones, skin and metabolism. One thread asserted that Peat gained roughly an inch in height in his 40s with DHEA supplementation; a reply expressed scepticism, noting that Peat made many other claims of rapid recovery.[5] Another thread pairs Peat's approach with raw animal-food diets.[6]

A 2024 Hacker News submission linking a mainstream news-site explainer titled "Ray Peat Diet: What Is It, and Does It Work?" shows the diet's reach beyond looksmaxxing forums into general nutrition discussion.[8] Grokipedia describes a wider "Peatarian" scene on Reddit and X and names podcasters and bloggers who promote the bioenergetic approach, and reports growing interest after Peat's death.[14]

Community opinion is divided; thread titles include both enthusiastic and critical reactions. Some posters treat the framework as a complete lifestyle; others take individual elements such as dairy, juice or avoiding seed oils.

Mary Enig, writing for the Weston A. Price Foundation in 2005, replied to Peat's position on essential fatty acids. She argued that the body cannot make essential fatty acids and that small amounts are required, while agreeing that large amounts of polyunsaturated fat can be harmful.[16]

Public-health bodies take a different position on sugar from Peat's. The World Health Organization's 2015 guideline recommends keeping free sugars below 10 percent of energy intake and says a reduction below 5 percent would bring additional benefits; it excludes sugars naturally present in fresh fruit, vegetables and milk.[17] A 2020 Cochrane review of saturated fat reduction reported that cutting saturated fat for at least two years lowered combined cardiovascular events, and that replacing it with polyunsaturated fat or carbohydrate appeared useful.[18] These findings bear on Peat's recommendations of coconut oil, butter and refined sugar, although neither source evaluates the Peat diet itself.

Peat's own articles are essays that rely heavily on animal, in-vitro and mechanistic studies and often argue against mainstream consensus, and Grokipedia notes that mainstream nutrition experts call his high-sugar advocacy pseudoscientific.[11][12][13][14] Proponents respond that the mainstream literature reflects commercial interests; Peat made that argument about sugar and heart-disease research in his own writing.[12]

No studies found. Published research exists on individual components of the diet, such as dairy intake, fruit consumption and dietary fat quality (for example the Cochrane review above), but no trial has tested the Ray Peat dietary pattern as a whole, or its effect on skin, hair or height.

timeline.event: Raymond Peat born, reportedly on 12 October in Santee, California.[14]
Peat begins work on progesterone and related hormones.[9]
Peat completes his University of Oregon biology dissertation after papers in Physiological Chemistry and Physics in 1971 and 1972.[9][14]
Nutrition for Women, the first of his listed books, appears.[14]
Progesterone in Orthomolecular Medicine published; From PMS to Menopause follows in 1997.[14]
Mary Enig publishes a reply to Peat on essential fatty acids for the Weston A. Price Foundation.[16]
Copyright dates on raypeat.com begin, which hosts his article archive.[9]
A dedicated Ray Peat discussion forum is reported to be established.[14]
Resource threads on Peat's views on nicotine and on DHEA and height circulate on looksmax.org.[4][5]
Peat dies on 24 November at age 86; tributes and renewed online interest follow.[14][15]
A mainstream explainer on the diet is submitted to Hacker News on 28 March.[8]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the Ray Peat diet is treated as a metabolism and hormone optimisation approach, with competing views on its credibility.[1][5]

claims.claim: The diet raises metabolism and corrects hormonal imbalance
claims.believers: Followers say pro-metabolic foods such as dairy, fruit and low PUFA intake improve metabolic function and hormones.[1]
claims.experts: No published trials have examined the diet as a whole.

claims.claim: Peat grew about an inch in his 40s using DHEA
claims.believers: A poster argued that Peat, as a scientist, would have measured himself accurately.[5]
claims.experts: No published study supports DHEA increasing adult height; another poster in the same thread was sceptical of the claim.[5]

claims.claim: Seed oils and polyunsaturated fats harm metabolism and skin
claims.believers: The guide's author lists removing polyunsaturated fats as one of the few strongly advised steps and rejects the idea that fatty acids are "essential"; Peat's own article makes the case at length.[7][11]
claims.experts: Mary Enig argued in 2005 that essential fatty acids are required in small amounts, and a 2020 Cochrane review found that replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat appeared useful for cardiovascular events.[16][18]

claims.claim: Refined sugar and fruit juice support metabolic rate and thyroid function
claims.believers: The guide describes Peat's promotion of refined sugar as one of the controversial but central parts of the approach; Peat argued that sugar is not the cause of obesity or diabetes.[7][12]
claims.experts: The WHO recommends limiting free sugars to under 10 percent of energy, excluding sugars naturally in fresh fruit and milk. No published trial has tested a Peat dietary pattern on metabolic rate or thyroid function.[17]

claims.claim: Daily milk, through its calcium, lowers body fat and stress
claims.believers: Peat's milk article links calcium intake to lower parathyroid hormone and less body fat, and followers adopt dairy as a staple.[13][1]
claims.experts: Peat's article relies on small, animal and mechanistic studies; no trial of the Peat dietary pattern exists.[13]

claims.claim: Salt and water retention can be managed by following Peat's views on sodium
claims.believers: A community thread collects Peat's writings on sodium and water retention.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested Peat's sodium recommendations as a looks intervention.

claims.claim: Nicotine supports a Peat-style metabolic approach
claims.believers: A resource thread on looksmax.org compiles material on Peat's views about nicotine.[4]
claims.experts: Health authorities generally describe nicotine as addictive and tobacco as harmful; no study has tested nicotine as part of this diet.

claims.claim: Combining the Peat diet with raw animal foods yields a stronger protocol
claims.believers: One thread presents a combined 'bioenergetic primal' stack of Peat's and a raw-food author's ideas.[6]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined the combination.

card.summary: Dairy, fruit, juice and low-PUFA eating from Raymond Peat's writings; popular for hormone claims, with no trials.
card.note: Hormone and height claims come from forum anecdotes; none have been tested in published studies.

quick.overview:
The Ray Peat diet is built around milk, fruit and juice, root vegetables, eggs, shellfish and saturated fats while avoiding polyunsaturated fats. Followers say it raises metabolism and balances hormones.
No clinical trials of the diet were found. Forum discussion mixes enthusiastic reports with scepticism.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say lowering PUFA intake and eating sugar-rich, dairy-rich foods supports thyroid function and metabolic rate and lowers estrogen. These mechanisms have not been tested in published studies of the diet.
quick.risks: No harms are documented. Users in forums mention hormone-related side effects anecdotally, and extreme claims such as height gain are unsupported by published research.

chain: Dairy, fruit, root vegetables and saturated fats; polyunsaturated fats avoided
Proponents say this supports thyroid function and metabolic rate
Proponents say hormone balance and energy improve
Users hope for clearer skin, a leaner physique and better-looking hair
angle.text: Followers eat a dairy, fruit and root-vegetable-heavy diet and avoid seed oils and other polyunsaturated fats, aiming for a higher metabolic rate and what they call better hormone balance. They connect this with skin quality, leanness and energy; these links are the community's own and have not been tested.
